prompt: Two staff officers disagree on the meaning of armor in a lecture. Which statement correctly captures the lesson?
options: Armor means only the plating of a vehicle and never refers to a force or a way of fighting
Armor is a combined arms force fighting mounted in armor-protected vehicles, and the word also means a defensive covering that affords protection
Armor means tank units fighting alone without the support of any other arm
Armor is a dismounted force that is protected by obstacles and prepared positions
explanation: Page 13 gives both senses of the word.

prompt: An armor task force is ordered to conduct internal security operations in peacetime. A staff officer says this contradicts its doctrinal mission. What is the correct assessment?
options: Contradiction: armor may conduct ISO only when it is attached to an infantry unit
No contradiction: armor may also conduct ISO, independently or in a task force, when higher headquarters requires it
Contradiction: ISO is permitted for armor only in wartime, never in a peacetime environment
No contradiction: ISO is the primary mission of armor and close combat is secondary
explanation: Page 14 says armor may also conduct ISO activities in peacetime as required by higher headquarters.

prompt: A staff organizes Philippine Army armor operations into mechanized infantry, cavalry and artillery operations. What correction does the lesson require?
options: Replace cavalry with engineer operations
Keep all three; the list is complete
Replace artillery with tank operations
Add artillery as a fourth sub-component
explanation: Page 15 lists mechanized infantry, cavalry and tank operations as the three sub-components.

prompt: A commander lists armor protection, firepower, mobility, flexibility and shock action as characteristics. His signal officer says one more is missing. Which?
options: Amphibious capability
Intensive and flexible communication
Air transportability
Independence from logistics
explanation: Page 20 lists six characteristics, including intensive and flexible communication.

prompt: An armored assault stalls because the company radios fail and orders cannot flow between vehicles. Which characteristic of armor is being degraded?
options: Intensive and flexible communication
Armor protection
Mobility
Firepower
explanation: Page 20 lists intensive and flexible communication as a characteristic of armor.

prompt: A mechanized infantry company has a headquarters of 2 officers and 15 enlisted and three platoons of 1 officer and 37 enlisted each. What is its total strength?
options: 5 officers and 111 enlisted
4 officers and 126 enlisted
6 officers and 126 enlisted
5 officers and 126 enlisted
explanation: Page 24 shows 5 officers and 126 enlisted; 15 + 3 x 37 = 126 and 2 + 3 = 5.

prompt: A mechanized infantry platoon has a headquarters and three squads. How are the soldiers distributed across the four AIFVs?
options: All three squads share two AIFVs while the platoon HQ travels on foot
The platoon leader and HQ ride in one AIFV and each squad rides in one of the other three
The platoon HQ is split across all four AIFVs and the squads ride separately
Each AIFV carries one squad and the HQ rides in a separate truck
explanation: Page 27 says the PL and HQ are mounted in one AIFV and the three squads in the other three.

prompt: During a dismount, the gunner and driver stay with the AIFV. A new lieutenant asks who forms the dismount team. Which answer is correct?
options: Only the squad leader and the automatic rifleman
The carrier team leader and the driver
All squad members who are not part of the carrier team
The platoon headquarters section
explanation: Page 26 says the dismount team is made up of all squad members not part of the carrier team.

prompt: A commander wants to assault unprepared, suppressed defenses and also infiltrate enemy positions. Which pairing of mode and task is correct?
options: Assault the suppressed defenses dismounted; infiltrate mounted
Do both tasks mounted in the AIFVs
Do both tasks dismounted on foot
Assault the suppressed defenses mounted; infiltrate dismounted
explanation: Page 28 lists assaulting suppressed defenses as mounted; page 29 lists infiltration as dismounted.

prompt: A battalion S3 keeps a mechanized infantry company mounted to defend against a dismounted attack and to secure obstacles against enemy breaching. What is the problem?
options: Both are mounted capabilities, so the plan is correct as written
Defending against dismounted attack is a tank task only
Both are dismounted capabilities, so the infantry must dismount to do them
Securing obstacles is a cavalry task only
explanation: Page 29 lists defending versus dismounted attack and securing obstacles as dismounted capabilities.

prompt: A commander orders a vehicle-mounted advance through dense, steep terrain. Which limitation applies, and which element is less affected?
options: AVs are unrestricted by terrain, while dismounted infantry are restricted to roads
AVs are restricted to certain avenues of approach, while dismounted infantry can cross terrain vehicles cannot
Infantry need time to dismount, while AVs move over any terrain faster than the infantry
AIFVs are as protected as tanks, so terrain is the only limit on the dismounted infantry
explanation: Pages 29-30 cover vehicle restrictions to avenues of approach and dismounted movement over untrafficable terrain.

prompt: During a dismount, soldiers pile up at the door, one rides on top of the AIFV, and another uses the AIFV as cover. Which statement is correct?
options: Only hiding behind the AV violates the SOPs
Only riding on top of the AV violates the SOPs
All three actions violate the dismounting SOPs
None violates the SOPs, since speed is of the essence
explanation: Page 31 says avoid piling at the door, no riders on top, and never hide behind an AV.

prompt: A squad has no enemy contact and the terrain is not favorable on the left. Which dismount does the lesson prescribe?
options: Dismount left
Dismount left under fire from the right
Mount from the right
Dismount right
explanation: Pages 33-34 give dismount right when terrain is not favorable on the left and no enemy contact.

prompt: An AIFV is hit by fire from the left while the squad is dismounting. Which response matches the lesson?
options: Dismount right, react to contact on the left, extricate out of the kill zone, then perform IAD
Dismount left toward the fire to engage it and remain in the kill zone until contact ends
Dismount right but wait for the fire to stop before reacting to the contact on the left
Stay mounted with the ramp closed until the contact on the left is over
explanation: Pages 40-44 give the dismount right procedure under fire from the left.

prompt: A cavalry troop is tasked with a long screen across dense forest and a major river. Which limitations does the lesson list?
options: High logistics requirements and mobility restricted by dense forest, steep rugged terrain and major water obstacles
Inability to conduct reconnaissance and a requirement to be reinforced for any security task
Limited mobility on roads and a restriction to daylight operations only
Reliance on infantry for security and an inability to operate as an economy of force
explanation: Page 61 lists high logistics requirements and terrain-restricted mobility as cavalry limitations.

prompt: A brigade commander asks what a separate cavalry troop is. Which statement is correct?
options: It belongs to the division cavalry squadron and works for the division commander
It is always a heavy unit, whatever the type of brigade it serves
It is an air cavalry unit that supports several brigades from the air
It is part of a separate light or armored brigade, heavy or light as the brigade is, and works for the brigade commander
explanation: Page 58 describes the separate cavalry troop.

prompt: A division commander uses cavalry to see the enemy early and to hold part of the front thinly. How does the lesson say this helps him?
options: Cavalry takes over the main attack so the division can avoid engagement
Cavalry holds all terrain permanently, so the division no longer needs a reserve
Cavalry replaces division reconnaissance units so staff planning is shortened
Situational awareness improves his ability to maneuver, and economy of force conserves combat power for engagement where he desires
explanation: Pages 53-54 give both fundamentals.

prompt: A staff assigns one unit to repel an enemy assault by close combat and counterattack, and another to neutralize the enemy by fire, maneuver and shock effect. Which units?
options: Tank first; mechanized infantry second
Cavalry first; tank second
Mechanized infantry first; tank second
Mechanized infantry first; cavalry second
explanation: Pages 18 and 17 give the mechanized infantry and tank missions.

prompt: A tank company must fight at night in an area where NBC hazards are possible. Which statement matches the lesson?
options: Tanks can operate only on a conventional battlefield, and thermal sights are issued to infantry
Tanks can operate on a conventional or NBC battlefield, and thermal sights enhance night fighting
Tanks cannot operate at night, and NBC hazards make tank support unusable
Tanks can fight at night only with illumination from other arms on a conventional battlefield
explanation: Page 66 lists these tank capabilities.

prompt: A planner assumes tanks will deploy to the theater under their own power and be sustained by infantry battalion trucks. Which limitations contradict this?
options: Tanks depend on flatbeds for deployment, and infantry units lack organic transport for tank CSS needs, especially Classes III, V and IX
Tanks depend on aircraft for deployment, and infantry units have enough transport for Class I only
Tanks deploy themselves, but their fuel needs are met by cavalry units
Tanks need no CSS support because they carry all supplies they need for the operation
explanation: Pages 67-68 list these tank limitations.

prompt: A tank company commander builds his plan. Which combination lists the planning considerations the lesson gives for tanks?
options: Surface danger zone, direct fire control measures, SBF positions and cover against enemy air
Where to dismount troops, weapon range, objective to combat trains distance and avenue restrictions
Indirect fire weapon support, weapon range, security operations and distance from main body
Surface danger zone, weapon range, security operations and the Ex-O as resource manager
explanation: Page 71 lists the tank planning considerations; the distractors mix in mechanized infantry and cavalry items.

prompt: A staff lists distance from main body, security operations and indirect fire weapon support as planning considerations. For which armor unit is this the list?
options: Tank
Mechanized infantry
Tank and mechanized infantry together
Cavalry
explanation: Page 70 lists these cavalry planning considerations.

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: A unit moves from the basic M113A2 APC to the RCWS version. Which change matches the lesson?
options: The RCWS replaces the .50 cal with a 25 mm cannon and extends maximum range to 6,800 m
The RCWS adds day and night cameras, range measuring and automatic target tracking, but its maximum range is 2,000 m versus 6,800 m
The RCWS removes the weapon from the vehicle and carries an unarmed crew
The RCWS has the same sights as the basic APC but a longer effective range of 2,000 m
explanation: Pages 73-74 compare the two M113A2 data sheets.

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: A commander needs a direct-fire vehicle with a 76 mm L23A1 main gun, 2,200 m effective direct fire range and a maximum ammunition load of 40 rounds. Which vehicle?
options: Sabrah Light Tank ASCOD II
M113A2 IFV Unmanned Turret System
Fire Support Vehicle (FSV)
Guarani 6x6 wheeled APC
explanation: Page 81 gives the FSV main gun and ranges.

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: Which pairing of vehicle and main weapon is correct according to the lesson?
options: Sabrah, 105 mm gun; M113A2 UTS, 25 mm Bush-Master; Guarani, 12.7 mm HMG
Sabrah, 76 mm gun; M113A2 UTS, 105 mm gun; Guarani, 25 mm Bush-Master
Sabrah, 12.7 mm HMG; M113A2 UTS, 76 mm gun; Guarani, 105 mm gun
Sabrah, 25 mm Bush-Master; M113A2 UTS, 12.7 mm HMG; Guarani, 105 mm gun
explanation: Pages 75, 82 and 83 give these main weapons.
